system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2128-11-22 23:28:00 to 2128-11-28 19:20:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with type 1 diabetes, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, and chronic gastroparesis was admitted for a flare of epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting, with a blood glucose over 700 mg/dL. She had stopped her sliding scale insulin due to poor intake and fear of hypoglycemia. Her pain improved with Dilaudid and lidocaine patch, and she was able to tolerate oral intake. A gastric emptying study confirmed delayed gastric emptying. Her insulin regimen was adjusted with an increase in nighttime Lantus to 14 units. Hypertension improved with restart of home medications. She developed pseudohyponatremia, which resolved with better glycemic control. PTH was elevated, prompting initiation of vitamin D. Despite ongoing hyperglycemia, she chose to be discharged home to care for her son, with a follow-up appointment scheduled in the diabetes clinic the next day. Port placement was deferred to outpatient setting.
problems: Hyperglycemia without evidence of diabetic ketoacidosis
End stage renal disease on hemodialysis
Personal history of noncompliance with medical treatment, presenting hazards to health

Findings paged to the covering house officer, Dr. ___,
at the time of discovery of 10:10 a.m. on the day of the exam and discussed
with him by Dr. ___ by telephone shortly thereafter.

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with type I diabetes mellitus, ESRD on
hemodialysis (RUE fistula), diabetic gastroparesis who has difficult
peripheral access requiring port placement. Multiple prior presentations with
diabetic ketoacidosis requiring resuscitation.

COMPARISON:  Chest radiograph ___.

TECHNIQUE:   OPERATORS: Dr. ___ radiology fellow) and
Dr. ___ radiology attending) performed the procedure. The
attending, Dr. ___ was present and supervising throughout the procedure.

ANESTHESIA: Moderate sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of
75mcg of fentanyl and 1 mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service
time of 30 min during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were
continuously monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse. 1% lidocaine
was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues overlying the access site.

MEDICATIONS: Fentanyl and midazolam. 1 g of cefazolin.

CONTRAST: 0 ml of Optiray contrast.

FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE: 3.6 min, 3 mGy

PROCEDURE
1. Left internal jugular approach chest single lumen Port-a-cath placement

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the explanation of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the
patient. The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and placed
supine on the exam table. A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___
protocol. The upper chest was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.

Under continuous ultrasound guidance, the left internal jugular vein was
compressible with moderate echogenic clot on the medial wall (suggestive of a
chronic clot) accessed using a micropuncture needle. Permanent ultrasound
images were obtained before and after intravenous access, which confirmed vein
patency. Subsequently a Nitinol wire was passed into the right atrium using
fluoroscopic guidance. The needle was exchanged for a micropuncture sheath.
The Nitinol wire was removed and a short ___ wire was advanced to make
appropriate measurements for catheter length. The ___ wire was then passed
distally into the IVC.

Next, attention was turned towards creation of a subcutaneous pocket over the
upper anterior chest wall. After instilling superficial and deeper local
anesthesia using lidocaine mixed with epinephrine, a 2.5 cm transverse
incision was made and a subcutaneous pocket was created by using blunt
dissection. The single lumen port was then connected to the catheter. The
catheter was tunneled from the subcutaneous pocket towards the venotomy site
from where it was brought out using a tunneling device. The port was then
connected to the catheter and checks were made for any leakage by accessing
the diaphragm using a non-coring ___ needle. No leaks were found.
The port was then placed in the subcutaneous pocket and secured with ___
Prolene sutures on either side. The venotomy tract was dilated using the
introducer of the peel-away sheath supplied. Following this, the peel-away
sheath was placed over the ___ wire through which the port was threaded into
the right side of the heart with the tip in the right atrium. The sheath was
then peeled away.
The subcutaneous pocket was closed in layers with ___ interrupted and ___
subcuticular continuous Vicryl sutures. ___ Vicryl suture and Steri-Strips
were used to close the venotomy incision site. Steri-Strips were applied over
the sutures. Final spot fluoroscopic image demonstrating good alignment of the
catheter and no kinking. The tip is in the right atrium.
The port was accessed using a non coring ___ needle and could be aspirated
and flushed easily. Sterile dressings were applied. The patient tolerated the
procedure well without immediate complication. The port was  left accessed as
requested.

FINDINGS: 

Chronic Medium-sized clot in the medial wall of the left IJ.  Final
fluoroscopic image showing port with catheter tip terminating in the right
atrium.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful placement of a single lumen chest Port-a-cath via the left internal
jugular venous approach. The tip of the catheter terminates in the right
atrium. The catheter is ready for use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I know you're feeling really unwell. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this awful stomach pain and I’ve been throwing up all day. I felt so weak and dizzy, so I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your blood sugar was extremely high—over 1300. That’s very dangerous. We’re calling it hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state. It can happen when your body doesn’t get enough insulin, especially if you’re not eating or drinking well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been able to keep anything down. I was scared to take my insulin because I didn’t want my sugar to drop too low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense, but when your sugar gets this high, it can cause serious problems. We’ve started you on an IV insulin drip to bring it down safely. We’ll also give you fluids to rehydrate you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I just want the nausea and pain to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you Zofran for nausea and hydromorphone for pain. You should start feeling better soon. We also noticed your potassium was very high—7.6—which can be dangerous for your heart. We’ve given you medication to bring it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that because of my kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Your kidneys aren’t filtering properly, so potassium builds up. You’re on dialysis, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, three times a week. I had one two days ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll schedule your next session while you’re here. We also did a chest X-ray because your oxygen levels dropped a bit. It showed some fluid in the lungs—likely from the high blood sugar and heart strain. We’re watching it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s something we need to manage. It’s called pulmonary edema. As your sugar comes down and we adjust your fluids, it should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood sugar has come down to 790—still high, but moving in the right direction. Your potassium is now normal. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. The pain is less, but I’m still nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing the insulin drip. The diabetes team is helping us adjust your long-acting insulin. We’re also checking your heart because your troponin was slightly elevated—likely from stress on the heart due to high blood pressure and sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t have chest pain though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. It means it’s probably not a heart attack, just strain. Your EKG was normal. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar is now 91—much better. But we’re seeing big swings. It went down to 62 this afternoon. We had to slow the insulin drip.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is it under control now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting there. We stopped the insulin drip and are switching back to injections. The diabetes team wants to increase your long-acting insulin to help prevent these highs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished your dialysis session. Your labs are improving. Your creatinine is down, and your fluid status is better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel less bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar has been fluctuating—sometimes in the 400s, sometimes low. We’re adjusting your insulin doses. We’re also increasing your labetalol for blood pressure. It was still in the 180s, so we’ve gone up to 400 mg three times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My usual pressure is high. I didn’t think it was a big deal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In the setting of high sugar and kidney disease, it adds extra strain. Getting it lower helps protect your heart and kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing much better. No more nausea or vomiting. You’ve been eating well. We’ve stopped the IV pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m actually hungry for the first time in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. That’s a sign your gastroparesis flare is resolving. We’ll keep you on metoclopramide to help your stomach empty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been talking about your frequent hospital visits and how hard it is to get IV access. The team thinks you’d benefit from a port.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like a permanent IV?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It’s a small device placed under the skin in your chest, connected to a vein. It’ll make getting IV access much easier in the future.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get sedation and local numbing. Most patients tolerate it well. It’s scheduled for tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The port placement went well. It’s in your left chest, and we’ve confirmed it’s working. You’ll have a small bandage, and it should heal in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can feel the bump, but it doesn’t hurt.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. We’ll show you how to care for it before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar is still running high—mostly in the 400s. We’ve adjusted your insulin again. You’ll be on 8 units of glargine with breakfast and 10 with dinner. Plus, 4 units of Humalog with meals, and a correction dose of 1 unit for every 50 points over 150.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s more than before. Will I go low?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor closely. The goal is to prevent highs like this admission. If your sugar drops below 70, eat 15 grams of carbs—like juice—and recheck in 15 minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re looking great. Your exam is normal, you’re eating well, and your labs are stable. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your dialysis schedule. Take your new insulin doses. Keep taking labetalol 600 mg three times a day for blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: 600 mg? That’s higher.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it helped bring your pressure down to the 140s. We want to keep it there. And please follow up with your endocrinologist within a week. Call if your sugar is over 400 or under 70.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You’ve made great progress. Take care of yourself, and we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. Your port site looks clean, blood pressure is 142/88, and you’re alert and walking fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send your discharge papers and prescriptions. A nurse will review everything with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to call the endocrinologist today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. That’s the best thing you can do for your health right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve learned a lot this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And we’re here to support you. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember, if you feel worse or your sugar is very high, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to be back here anytime soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. This stay was tough, but you’re stronger now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel like I understand my body better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. Keep asking questions and taking your meds. You’ve got this.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with type 1 diabetes, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, and gastroparesis was admitted for severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and hyperglycemia with a glucose over 1300 mg/dL, diagnosed as hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state. She was treated in the MICU with IV fluids and an insulin drip, which was later transitioned to subcutaneous insulin. Her potassium was elevated at 7.6 and managed with medication. She experienced fluctuating glucose levels, requiring multiple insulin dose adjustments. Her blood pressure, initially in the 190s, improved with labetalol titration to 600 mg TID. A chest X-ray showed pulmonary edema, likely due to fluid overload and hyperglycemia, which resolved with treatment. She underwent successful placement of a left internal jugular port-a-cath due to chronic IV access difficulties. Her gastroparesis symptoms resolved with supportive care, and she tolerated oral intake. She was discharged home with updated insulin regimen, continued antihypertensives, and instructions to follow up with her endocrinologist.
